Gautama
(‘descendent of [the sage] गोतम’)
------------------------------------------
Being a patronymic title, the word ‘Gautama’ can apply to anyone supposed to be a descendant of the sage गोतम. We come across several Gautamas in the Vedic literature like the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and also in quite a few उपनिषद्स्. Here the गौतम may be a sage giving some important teaching or may have just been mentioned in the lists of vaṁśas or genealogies.
Of all the Gautamas, गौतम the son of the sage दीर्घतमस् and the husband of अहल्या is the most celebrated one. He is considered as one among the सप्तर्षिस् (the Seven Sages) and a गोत्र-pravartaka or the originator of a particular lineage. Of his many achievements, the more important ones may be listed as follows: scholarly conversations with other great sages like अत्रि, अङ्गिरस् and यम (the god of death); training the sage उदङ्क who was his disciple and Śatānanda, his own son; protecting the people during a severe famine; originating the sacred river गोदावरी (also called Gotamī river) by the power of his prayer and so on.
Akṣapāda, the author of the Nyāya-sūtras (the basic work of the न्याय system of Philosophy) was also known as गौतम.
There is an ancient work called Gautama Dharmasūtras. This गौतम probably belonged to the period 600-400 B. C. His work has been quoted as an authority by later writers on the धर्म-śāstras.

Gautama Dharmasūtras
------------------------------------------
Hinduism has always considered धर्म (foundational मोरलित्य् and एथिच्स्) as a basic value which must cover all aspects of life, individual as well as social. One of the earliest classes of scriptures dealing with धर्म is the dharmasūtra literature.
The Dharmasūtras of गौतम has been considered a quite ancient (600-400 B. C.)—perhaps, the oldest—dharmasūtra work and authoritative. It has been held in high esteem by the later writers of धर्मशास्त्रस्.
There is reason to believe that the Dharmasūtras of गौतम is an independent work and not a part of the कल्पसूत्रस्.
The sage गौतम probably belonged to the Rāṇāyānīya school of the Sāmaveda.
This work has a bhāṣya or commentary by मस्करिन् (A.
) and another one called Mitākṣarā by हरदत्त (A.

).
The Gautama Dharmasūtras is written entirely in prose and has 28 chapters.
A brief summary of the contents can now be attempted:
Sources of धर्म; details of the उपनयन sacrament; the four āśramas; rules concerning मर्रिअगे and the duties of a householder; the पञ्चमहायज्ञस् or the five daily sacrifices; the duties of the four varṇas; राजधर्म or the duties and responsibilities of a king; च्रिमे अन्द् पुनिस्ह्मेन्त्; rules concerning law-suits; śrāddhas or obsequial ceremonies; rules regulating ड़ोओद् and eating; on women; sins and their expiations; penances; पर्तितिओन् of property and related matters.
